tagline: Black soil, golden domes, wide steppe
overview:
Ukraine is the largest country lying entirely within Europe, roughly the size of Texas, stretching from the Carpathian Mountains in the west to the Russian border in the east and south to the Black Sea. Its land is famous for chernozem, a deep black soil so fertile that Ukraine has long been called a breadbasket, sending wheat, corn, barley and sunflower oil to many countries.

Before 2022 about 41 million people lived in Ukraine; millions have since left the country or moved within it. Ukrainian is the state language, a Slavic language written in the Cyrillic alphabet, and many people also speak Russian. Ukraine is a republic with an elected president and parliament. Kyiv, the capital, stands on the Dnipro River and is one of the oldest cities in eastern Europe, known for gold-domed churches and a very deep metro. Russia began a full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the war continues.
landAndNature: Most of Ukraine is flat or gently rolling steppe and farmland, a plain of wheat and enormous fields of sunflowers that turn to follow the sun. The Carpathian Mountains in the west are wooded and green, rising to Hoverla at 2,061 meters and holding some of Europe's largest surviving beech forests, where brown bears, wolves and lynx live. The Dnipro River runs the length of the country to the Black Sea, whose northern shore has sandy spits, salt lakes and the marshy Danube delta where pelicans breed. Around the abandoned Chornobyl nuclear plant, empty of people since 1986, wolves, boar and wild horses now roam freely.
peopleAndCulture: Borscht, a beet soup served with sour cream and garlic bread, is the best-known Ukrainian dish and is listed by UNESCO as cultural heritage; varenyky dumplings follow close behind. Embroidered shirts called vyshyvanky carry patterns that differ from region to region and are worn with pride on holidays. Pysanky, eggs decorated with wax and dye in fine geometric designs, are made at Easter. Layered folk singing and the many-stringed bandura belong to old traditions, while Kyiv has a lively modern music scene. Soccer, boxing and chess are popular, and Ukrainian boxers have held world heavyweight titles.
history: Kyiv grew into the center of Kyivan Rus, a powerful medieval state that adopted Christianity in 988. Mongol armies destroyed it in 1240, and the lands were later ruled by Poland-Lithuania, by Cossack hosts, and by the Russian Empire. In 1932 and 1933 a famine known as the Holodomor, caused by Soviet grain seizures, killed millions of Ukrainians. Ukraine suffered enormously in World War II, and the Chornobyl reactor exploded in 1986. Independence came when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and fighting began in the eastern regions; in February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion, and the war has continued since.
funFacts: Ukraine's black soil, called chernozem, covers much of the country and is among the most fertile farmland on Earth.
Ukraine grows more sunflowers than almost any other country and is a leading supplier of sunflower oil.
Kyiv's Arsenalna station is one of the deepest metro stations in the world, about 105 meters underground.
The world's largest cargo aircraft, the Antonov An-225 Mriya, was built in Ukraine and destroyed in 2022.
The bandura, Ukraine's national instrument, has more than 60 strings and is held upright against the player's chest.
